syllabusTopics: Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes): preparation from haloalkanes (reduction and Wurtz reaction), decarboxylation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkene and alkyne
Chemical properties of alkanes: substitution reactions (halogenation, nitration and sulphonation only), oxidation of ethane
Unsaturated hydrocarbons (Alkenes): preparation by dehydration of alcohol, dehydrohalogenation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkyne
Chemical properties of alkenes: addition reaction with HX (Markovnikov's addition and peroxide effect), H2O, O3, H2SO4 only
Alkynes: preparation from carbon and hydrogen, 1,2-dibromoethane, chloroform/iodoform only
Chemical properties of alkynes: addition reaction with H2, HX, H2O; acidic nature (action with sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3 and ammoniacal Cu2Cl2)
Test of unsaturation (ethene and ethyne): bromine water test and Baeyer's test
Comparative studies of physical properties of alkane, alkene and alkyne
Kolbe's electrolysis methods for the preparation of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Kolbe's electrolysis forges C–C bonds with electricity. In **sodium acetate solution (Pt electrodes)** the **anode** oxidises acetate — **CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃· + CO₂ + e⁻** — and methyl radicals couple to **ethane**, while the **cathode** makes H₂ and NaOH: **2CH₃COONa + 2H₂O → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Kolbe electrolysis converts carboxylates to hydrocarbons at the anode by decarboxylative radical coupling; dicarboxylates yield alkenes and alkynes."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Succinate's self-coupling*** — one molecule, two anodic exits, one triple bond: the dicarboxylate needs no partner because its two ends were already married.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Electricity Builds Hydrocarbons Kolbe's electrolysis passes current through a **carboxylate solution**: at the anode, carboxylate ions surrender electrons, lose CO₂, and **couple into hydrocarbons**. Sodium acetate gives **ethane**; succinic acid gives **ethyne**; a suitable salt can even deliver **ethene** — electrolysis as a C–C bond factory.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate → alkane - Electrolyte: **concentrated sodium acetate solution**; electrodes: platinum; product at **anode**. - **CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃· + CO₂ + e⁻** (anodic oxidation); **2CH₃· → CH₃–CH₃** (ethane). - Cathode: **2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻** (hydrogen evolves); solution turns alkaline. - Overall: **2CH₃COONa + 2H₂O → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Anode = product (radical coupling); cathode = H2 + NaOH. Acetate → ethane; propionate → butane (2×R carbons); succinate → ethyne. CO2 is the carboxyl carbon's exit.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Electrolysis as a bond forge: the anode strips electrons and CO2 from carboxylates, and the freed radicals couple — the current literally welds carbons together.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Kolbe electrolysis: anodic decarboxylative coupling. Sodium acetate (conc, Pt electrodes): anode CH3COO- -> CH3. + CO2 + e-; 2CH3. -> C2H6; cathode 2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH-; overall 2CH3COONa + 2H2O -> C2H6 + 2CO2 + H2 + 2NaOH (solution becomes NaOH). Rule: product carbons = 2 x (R carbons); propionate -> n-butane.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Kolbe's 1845 synthesis was the first total synthesis of an organic compound from elements — acetic acid from C, H, O — the ancestor of all synthetic organic chemistry.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Predict the Kolbe product of sodium propionate.** — Sodium propionate is **CH₃CH₂COONa**. At the anode each propionate ion decarboxylates: **CH₃CH₂COO⁻ → C₂H₅· + CO₂ + e⁻**, and two **ethyl radicals couple**: **2C₂H₅· → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃** — **n-butane**.…

Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Kolbe electrolysis** | Anodic decarboxylative coupling of carboxylates to hydrocarbons | acetate → ethane | | **Anodic oxidation** | Loss of electron(s) at the anode: RCOO⁻ → R· + CO₂ | the coupling engine | | **Dicarboxylate electrolysis** | Both ends decarboxylate; intramolecular coupling…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 The anode is the workshop - Every carbon–carbon bond of the product is forged **at the anode**: RCOO⁻ surrenders its electron, CO₂ departs, the naked R· radicals meet and couple. The cathode merely makes hydrogen and base. ### 4.2 Counting carbons - Two acetates (C₂ each) − two carboxyl carbons → **C₂ ethane**.…  ·  ## 5.
